1.sense: The surah opens by swearing on the sky, and not on the sky as empty space but on the fixed formations set into it. Burj in ordinary Arabic is a tower or a fortified station, so the first thing the listener is told to look at is a height that has been built and garrisoned.

notes.t: What al-buruj names here is read more than one way. The great stars and constellations, the mansions the sun and moon pass through, and the guarded gates of the sky have all been held. The word itself is the word for a fortress tower, and every reading keeps that.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the constellations, the stations and the gates without settling on one

notes.t: An oath sworn on the sky as a structure sets the frame for what follows. The surah is about a hole dug in the ground and what was done inside it, and it begins by naming the thing above that ground.
The Qur'an uses the same word for the sky in two other places, both times in the context of what has been placed there deliberately.

links.why: We placed constellations in the sky and made it pleasing to those who look
the same word again, joined to a lamp and a shining moon

2.sense: The second oath is on a day that has not happened yet, and it is identified by nothing except the fact that it was promised. Its whole guarantee is that somebody said it would come.

notes.t: Mawʿud is a passive participle: the Day that was promised, not the Day that promises. It is fixed by an act of speech already completed, which is how an oath can be sworn on something still in the future.
The exegetes are effectively agreed that the promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, and the surah confirms it by spending the rest of its length on what is settled then.
The Qur'an makes the keeping of the promise a matter of Allah's own description rather than of circumstance.

links.why: a Day for which mankind will be gathered and which will be witnessed
the Hour is coming, and the reason it is kept hidden

3.sense: The third oath is on a witness and on the thing witnessed, and both are left indefinite. The surah is about to describe people who sat and watched, so the oath lands on the act of watching before any watcher has been named.

notes.t: This is one of the most contested pairs in the Qur'an. Friday and the Day of Arafah, the Prophet ﷺ and his community, the angels and the deeds they record, and every witness together with everything witnessed have all been argued for by serious exegetes.
notes.src: at-Tabari lists a long series of positions and prefers the general reading

notes.t: Both words are indefinite in the Arabic, which keeps them open rather than pointing at one appointed thing. The general reading is also the one that fits what the surah does four verses later, when it calls a crowd on the rim of a trench witnesses.
The root sh-h-d runs through this surah three times in nine verses: here, of the killers, and finally of Allah. The oath is planting the word it will use against them.

links.why: the same root turned on the men sitting at the fire
what it will be like when a witness is brought from every nation

4.sense: The verdict is delivered before the story. The people who dug the trench are condemned in the first words spoken about them, so what follows is not an inquiry with an open ending but the reading of an already settled charge.

notes.t: Qutila is literally killed, used in Arabic as a curse formula the way a speaker might say may he be finished. The Qur'an uses it in the same way of the falsifiers and of ungrateful man.
Ukhdud is a long cut in the ground, from the root khadd, which also gives the word for a cheek. The picture is a furrow, something dug the length of a field rather than a pit.

The Qur'an gives these people no place, no date and no names. Many exegetes attach the account to Najran in southern Arabia and to the long report of the boy, the king, the monk and the sorcerer, which ends with believers thrown into a fire. That identification comes from the historians, not from these verses.
notes.src: the long report is in Muslim 3005 and names no location; the Najran attribution is the work of later historians

links.why: the same curse formula used of those who guess at the truth
destroyed is man, how ungrateful he is

5.sense: The trench is named a second time, now by what filled it. Fuel has to be cut, carried and fed in, so the description turns the killing into a supplied project rather than a flare of temper.

notes.t: Waqud is the material burned, not the flame that comes off it. Naming the fuel names the labour: somebody gathered the wood and somebody kept feeding it while the seats were occupied.
The construction dhat, possessed of, is the same one used of the sky in verse one. Both the sky and the trench are introduced by what they hold, and the surah is about to weigh one against the other.
The Qur'an uses the fuel image for the Fire of the next life, and there the fuel is people and stones rather than wood.

links.why: the Fire whose fuel is men and stones
the kindled fire of Allah, described by its burning rather than its size

6.sense: The detail the surah picks out is the sitting. They were not fighting, not fleeing, not carrying out an order in a hurry. They had taken seats around the edge, which is what a person does when he expects to be somewhere for a while.

notes.t: Quʿud is the plural of an active participle, not a past tense verb. Arabic uses that form for a state held rather than an act completed, so the men are left sitting inside the sentence.
The preposition ʿalayha, over it, puts them on the rim looking down into the trench. The verse spends its words on posture and vantage point and says nothing at all about the people in the fire.
The seating is what makes this a scene rather than an atrocity report. A crowd that sits has decided to be an audience, and the next verse names it as one.

links.why: on that Day it is the believers on the couches, looking on
the verse that tells you what they were doing while they sat

7.sense: The word from the third oath comes back and is fastened onto them. They are witnesses, and the thing they witness is their own act, so the case against them is built out of the fact that they were present and watching.

notes.t: Shuhud answers shahid in verse three. The oath was sworn on a witness, and six verses later the surah has produced the ugliest kind of witness there is: one who watches a thing he is himself doing.
The verb yafʿalun is present tense inside a past frame. In Arabic that keeps the action running in front of the listener instead of closing it off as finished.
The victims are named only by their faith, al-mu'minin. No tribe, no age, no number. The surah gives them the single description that the next verse turns into the whole indictment.

links.why: the oath this verse cashes in
the Day their own tongues and hands and feet give evidence against them

8.sense: The charge sheet is one line long. Nothing was stolen, nothing was broken, nobody was harmed. The offence was belief. Then the verse names the One believed in with two attributes that answer the situation exactly: He is not weak, and He is worth what it cost.

notes.t: Naqama is to find fault with something and hold it against a person. The Arabic frame they held nothing against them except that is a standard way of showing that the stated grievance is no grievance at all.

The same construction is put in the mouths of Pharaoh's magicians after they believed, and again in a challenge to the People of the Book. In all three places the accusation collapses as soon as it is stated in full.

Al-Aziz is the one nothing overpowers and al-Hamid is the one who deserves praise. Placed at the end of this verse they say that the killers were not stronger than the object of that belief, only quicker.

links.why: you take revenge on us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord
do you resent us for nothing but that we believed in Allah

9.sense: The description of the One they believed in continues, and it closes on the same root a third time. The men on the rim thought they were the only witnesses in the place, and that whatever they agreed among themselves afterwards would be the record.

notes.t: Shahid is the third appearance of sh-h-d in nine verses: an unnamed witness in the oath, the killers as witnesses of their own act, and now Allah as witness over all of it. The surah has been assembling this word from the start.
A king ordered that trench dug and held a stretch of one province. The verse answers by naming what the other party owns, and the two quantities are not on the same scale.
The Qur'an states elsewhere that no deed is done except with Allah present as witness to it, and it says this to the Prophet ﷺ about his own affairs first.

links.why: you do not do a deed without Us being witnesses over you while you are in it
no private conversation of three without Him as the fourth

10.sense: The sentence widens from one trench to a standing rule. Anyone who burns believers and does not turn back afterwards receives two named punishments. The clause about repentance is left sitting in the middle of the threat, where it cannot be missed.

notes.t: Fatana is originally to put metal into fire to see what it is made of. The word carries persecution and testing in one movement, which is exactly what the trench was: a fire that asked a question.

Al-Hasan al-Basri is quoted on this verse saying to look at the generosity in it: they burned His friends alive and He is still calling them to repent. It is a scholar's remark on the wording, and the wording is the text's.
notes.src: quoted from al-Hasan al-Basri by Ibn Kathir in his commentary on this verse

notes.t: Believing men and believing women are listed separately rather than under one plural. The verse counts the victims in both columns instead of letting the masculine plural cover them.

links.why: do not despair of the mercy of Allah, said to those who went furthest
repentance that turns the record itself over

11.sense: Against a trench of fire, gardens with water running underneath them. The pairing is deliberate and so is the last word. This is called the great winning, and it is said about people who were burned alive in front of a seated crowd and who by every visible measure lost.

notes.t: Fawz is the word for coming out of a contest safe and ahead. Applied here it reverses the verdict of the day itself, when the men with the fuel walked home and the believers did not.
The usual Qur'anic pairing is al-fawz al-ʿazim, the immense attainment. Here it is al-fawz al-kabir, the great one, and the phrase in this exact form occurs only in this place.
The Qur'an ties the same gardens to the same two conditions, faith and righteous work, in dozens of places, and calls the result an attainment there too.

links.why: the same gardens and the same word for winning
whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has won

12.sense: The surah turns and speaks to one person for the first time, and what it says to him is about grip. Batsh is not a sentence handed down from a distance. It is a hand closing on something.

notes.t: Batsh is a violent seizing, the word for grabbing a man by force. Arabic has quieter words for punishment and the verse does not use them.

Your Lord, said to the Prophet ﷺ, places this sentence in the middle of a small and pressed community rather than in the mouth of a state. The consolation is that the grip belongs to the side that currently has none.
The same root names the day of the greatest seizing, where it is given as the direct answer to a people who thought the matter was closed.

links.why: the Day We seize with the greatest seizure
the grip of your Lord on a town that wronged, said with a different verb

13.sense: The grip in the verse before is backed here by two verbs. A power that could only destroy would have no answer to a trench full of dead believers. One that starts a thing and returns it does.

notes.t: Both verbs are given without an object, which leaves them general. He begins and He brings back, and the sentence does not restrict what the thing is.
Yuʿid is the standard Qur'anic term for the second creation, and the Qur'an argues from it: bringing a thing back is the easier of the two by any reckoning a human being has.
Placed between the severe seizing of verse twelve and the forgiveness of verse fourteen, this verse is the hinge. Restoration is what makes both the threat and the pardon mean anything.

links.why: He begins creation then repeats it, and that is easier for Him
the return of all of you together, stated as a promise in truth

14.sense: Two verses after the severe grip, two names of pardon and warmth. Wadud is built on wudd, the ordinary affection that passes between people, and it is not a distant word.

notes.t: Al-Wadud occurs twice in the whole Qur'an. Here, and on the lips of Shuʿayb telling his people that his Lord is Merciful and Loving while they are threatening to stone him.
Whether wadud means the One who loves or the One who is loved is discussed by the grammarians, since the pattern faʿul can carry either. Most carry the active sense, and some hold both at once.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries He loves His obedient servants; others read it as the One His servants love

notes.t: The placement is the argument. The names of pardon are given to the same audience that was just told about the seizing, and in the same breath as the promise that He brings things back.

links.why: the only other place the name al-Wadud appears
affection appointed for those who believe and work righteousness

15.sense: A throne is named, and the surah has already shown a man on one. A king ordered a furrow dug and sat above it. The One described here owns the Throne and everything the Throne stands over.

notes.t: The canonical readings differ on the last vowel. With damma, al-Majidu describes the Owner; with kasra, al-Majidi describes the Throne. Both are transmitted and both are recited. The reading in this Mushaf has the damma.
notes.src: the ten readings split on the final vowel; Hafs from Asim reads al-Majīdu

notes.t: Majd in Arabic joins two things English separates: greatness of standing, and generosity with what that standing allows. A majid is not merely exalted, he gives.
The Qur'an attaches the Throne to Allah repeatedly and always with an adjective of scale, which keeps the word from being read as a seat.

links.why: Lord of the mighty Throne, given as what to say when people turn away
the Throne named noble at the close of an argument about creation

16.sense: The word is in the intensive pattern, so it is not one who does but one who does and keeps doing. Nothing stands between the intention and the event, which is the answer to a story in which men with fuel and seats appeared to have the last word.

notes.t: Faʿʿal is the Arabic shape for a settled occupation. It is the pattern behind khabbaz for a baker and najjar for a carpenter: not one who once baked, but the one whose work this is.
The same phrase closes a passage in Surah Hud, where it is said about the fate of two groups after the Day, and there too it comes at the end of a stretch about outcomes nobody can appeal.

Three verses have now described Allah by what He does rather than by what He is like: He begins and brings back, He forgives and loves, He carries out what He intends. The surah is answering an audience that had watched action and been impressed by it.

links.why: the identical phrase, closing a passage on the two destinations
His command when He intends a thing

17.sense: A question is put to the listener, and it already assumes the answer. The surah turns from a trench nobody could locate to two names every Arab could recite from memory.

notes.t: Hal ataka is a Qur'anic opening formula for a story the audience half knows. It is used the same way at the head of Surah Al-Ghashiya and before the account of Musa in the valley.
Junud means armies, and it is the word chosen instead of kings, peoples or nations. It names the thing about them that mattered to onlookers, which is the thing about to be shown as no protection.
Hadith here means an account or a report. The Qur'an uses the ordinary word for news to introduce two of the most catastrophic endings in its history sections.

links.why: the same question used to open a surah about the Day
has the account of Musa come to you, put to the same listener

18.sense: Two names and nothing else. One ran the largest state in its region and the other cut houses out of solid rock. Neither story is retold, because the audience already had both and the point is the ending, not the plot.

notes.t: Pharaoh went down in water and Thamud were taken by a cry and a shaking of the ground. Two different sorts of strength, two different instruments, one result each.
The Qur'an pairs these two elsewhere as the standard examples of a people who could not be argued with and were removed anyway. In Surah Al-Fajr they are named in consecutive verses.
Thamud is told at length in the surah that sits six places after this one, which is why the two reward being read together: this verse gives the name, Ash-Shams gives the day it ended.

links.why: the full Thamud account, from the denial to the levelling
the same two named side by side, with the rock cutting specified

19.sense: The examples did not land. The verse does not say the deniers hold an opinion or made an argument. It says they are inside denial, the way a person is inside a room, which describes a location rather than a conclusion.

notes.t: Bal is the particle of correction. It cancels the expectation raised by the question two verses earlier: yes, the account reached them, and no, it changed nothing.
Fi takdhib uses the preposition of containment. Arabic could have said they deny, and instead the verse makes denial the space they occupy and leaves them standing in it.
The Qur'an distinguishes elsewhere between not knowing and rejecting what one has recognised, and it puts the deniers of the Prophet ﷺ in the second category by name.

links.why: they do not call you a liar, they reject the signs of Allah knowingly
they denied while their own selves were convinced

20.sense: They are inside denial and He is around the outside of it. Wara' means behind and it also means beyond, and either way the picture is of a wall at their back that they have not turned round to see.

notes.t: Muhit is the participle of a verb meaning to surround on every side. The same root gives al-muhit, the name Arabic uses for the ocean that goes all the way round.
This answers verse six precisely. Men sat around a trench and believed they had it surrounded, and the surah closes the geometry by putting somebody around them.
The Qur'an states the encompassing directly and without a metaphor at the end of Surah Fussilat, where it is offered as the last word of a long argument about signs.

links.why: He encompasses all things, given as the closing statement of an argument
the men who thought they were the ones doing the surrounding

21.sense: The second correction in three verses. Whatever they have decided to call this, it is a recitation that carries glory, and the word used for it is the same word used six verses earlier for the Owner of the Throne.

notes.t: Majid ties the Book to the Throne by vocabulary. The surah has spent its second half naming what cannot be reached by men with fuel, and it ends the list with the recitation itself.
Qur'an means a reading aloud, from qara'a. The Book names itself by the act of being recited rather than by being written down, which is what the last verse then has to correct.
Other surahs swear by this Book with an adjective attached, and the choice of adjective changes with the argument being made.

links.why: an oath sworn by the glorious Qur'an at the head of a surah about resurrection
the recitation described as noble in the middle of a similar denial

22.sense: The last words of the surah put the recitation somewhere out of reach. Men with wood and a trench could burn bodies in an afternoon and could not touch this, which is the whole distance the surah has been measuring.

notes.t: The canonical readings differ on the last vowel. In the genitive it is the tablet that is guarded; in the nominative it is the Qur'an that is guarded, wherever the tablet may be. This Mushaf reads the genitive.
notes.src: the ten readings split on the final vowel of maḥfūẓ; Hafs from Asim reads the genitive

notes.t: Lawh is an ordinary word for a board or plank. The Qur'an uses the plural of it for the timbers of Nuh's ship, which keeps the image from floating away into abstraction.
The surah opened with a sky held in position by towers and closes with a Book held in position on a tablet. Both ends are about something fixed above a world where nothing was.

links.why: We sent down the Reminder and We are its guardian
in a Book kept concealed, said of the same recitation

1.sense: Seven things are sworn by in the first seven verses of this surah, the longest run of oaths at the head of anything in the Qur'an. The first is the sun, and specifically its duha, the stretch of morning when the light has climbed high enough to be full but has not yet turned hard.

notes.t: Duha is a named part of the day in Arabic, not a general word for brightness. It sits after sunrise and before the sun stands at its highest, and a whole prayer takes its name from it.
The Prophet ﷺ named this surah among the ones Muʿadh should have led his people with, after Muʿadh had kept them standing too long with a longer one.
notes.src: Bukhari 705

notes.t: The oaths run outward and then inward: sun, moon, day, night, sky, earth, and then a single self. The sequence narrows all the way down to one person, and that is where the surah puts its claim.

links.why: a whole surah opening on the same word for the morning light
the sun made a lamp and the moon a light in the same sentence

2.sense: The moon is sworn by at the moment it comes after the sun. Its light is borrowed and its position in the sentence is second, and the oath takes it at exactly that point rather than at the full moon.

notes.t: Tala means to follow, and it is the same verb behind tilawa, the recitation of a text. A reciter follows the words one after another the way the moon follows the sun, which is why the Qur'an uses one root for both.
What the following consists of is read two ways: the moon rising as the sun sets in the middle of the month, or the moon taking its light from the sun and so coming after it in that sense.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both the timing reading and the light reading

notes.t: The pronoun in talaha refers back to the sun, which in Arabic is grammatically feminine while the moon is masculine. The surah keeps every one of its fifteen verses ending on that same feminine ha.

links.why: the sun given as a shining thing and the moon as a derived light
neither is permitted to overtake the other

3.sense: Day is sworn by as the thing that shows the sun, rather than the other way round. The order is turned deliberately, so that time and the light in it are set beside each other instead of one being made to explain the other.

notes.t: Jalla is to polish something until it shows clearly. The same root gives the word for a bride being unveiled at her wedding, and for a matter becoming plain after being obscure.
The object of jallaha is disputed. Most exegetes take it as the sun, following the previous verses. Others read it as the earth or the world, which is not named anywhere in the sentence.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries both the sun and the unnamed world as the referent of the pronoun

notes.t: A neighbouring surah puts day and night in the same order with almost the same verbs, which is one reason the two are usually read as a pair.

links.why: by the day when it shows itself, two surahs later
He darkened its night and brought out its morning light

4.sense: Night is sworn by as an act of covering rather than as an absence. Ghisha is the verb for pulling a cloth over a thing, so darkness is described as something laid on top of light, not as what is left when light stops.

notes.t: The verb switches tense here. The two verses before used the past, talaha and jallaha, and this one uses the present, yaghshaha. Arabic uses that shift to make an action recurrent rather than finished.
The same root gives ghishawa, the covering laid over the eyes of those who will not see, and al-ghashiya, the event that comes over everything at the end.
A covering can be lifted, and the surah is building toward a verse about a soul buried out of sight. Night is the first thing in it that hides something without destroying it.

links.why: by the night when it covers, the identical verb opening the next surah but one
by the night as it closes in

5.sense: The sky and the building of it are sworn by together. The verb is the ordinary one for putting up a house, so the sky is presented as a structure with a builder and not as an expanse that happens to be there.

notes.t: The particle ma is normally used for things and man for persons, so its use here is discussed. Many read it as making a verbal noun, and the building of it; others read it as the One who built it, since ma can carry that in Arabic when the description matters more than the identity.
notes.src: az-Zamakhshari prefers the verbal noun reading; at-Tabari carries both

notes.t: Bana gives bina', a building, and the Qur'an calls the sky exactly that in one of its earliest arguments for worshipping the One who made it.
Three verses have sworn by light and time, things nobody handles. This one moves to construction, an act every listener in Mecca had watched being done by hand.

links.why: the earth a bed and the sky a building, in the same breath
We built the heaven with power and We are its expander

6.sense: The earth and the spreading of it. Taha is a rare verb, glossed by the lexicographers as driving a thing outward and away in every direction, and it does not occur anywhere else in the Qur'an.

notes.t: Taha appears once in the entire Qur'an, here. Its near twin daha, used of the earth in Surah An-Naziʿat, is also rare, and both carry outward extension rather than flattening.
Sky then earth, built then spread. Each of the two verses gives its half of the world a verb of workmanship, which keeps the oath from being an appeal to scenery.
The lexicographers explain taha with the image of pushing something out until it lies open in front of you, the way a rug is sent across a floor.

links.why: the earth spread out after that, with the sister verb
Allah made the earth for you a thing spread open

7.sense: The last of the seven oaths leaves the sky and the earth and comes down to a single self, and it is left indefinite. Not the soul, but a soul, which is any of them, and includes the one holding the page.

notes.t: Every previous oath took a definite noun: the sun, the moon, the day, the night, the sky, the earth. This one alone is indefinite, nafsin, and the narrowing from six named enormities to one unnamed person is the work of the whole opening.
Sawwa is to make even, balanced and complete. The Qur'an uses it for the forming of the human being, where it is followed immediately by the mention of proportion in the limbs.

The grammarians differ over where the answer to these oaths begins. Most take verse nine as the answer with its opening lam left out, since Arabic drops it when the statement is long; a few hold that the answer is omitted altogether.
notes.src: the grammarians of tafsir differ; the majority read verse nine as the answer with an elided lam

links.why: who created you, then proportioned you, then balanced you
then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit

8.sense: With the shaping came the knowledge of both directions. The verse does not say a rule book was handed over. It says the recognition of what breaks and what protects was put inside the self at the level where a person does not have to be taught.

notes.t: Ilham is knowledge placed into a self without instruction from outside. The root also gives iltiham, swallowing something whole, which is the physical picture underneath: it goes in without being chewed over.

Fujur comes from a verb meaning to split open, used of a dam giving way. Taqwa comes from wiqaya, a shield or a guard. So the pair is bursting out against holding in, and both are described as native to the same self.
The Prophet ﷺ asked for the second half of this verse directly: O Allah, give my soul its taqwa and purify it, for You are the best of those who purify it, You are its Guardian and its Master.
notes.src: Muslim 2722

links.why: and We showed him the two elevations
We guided him to the road, whether grateful or ungrateful

9.sense: The answer to seven oaths is one short sentence about a person nobody can see. Everything sworn by was enormous, and what it was sworn over is what a single self quietly does with itself.

notes.t: Aflaha is from falah, which the lexicographers connect to splitting the ground open. The Arabic word for a ploughman, fallah, comes from the same root, and the picture is of breaking soil so that something can come up through it.
Zakka carries cleaning and growing at once. Zakah is a payment that takes from a pile and is described as increasing it, and the same verb is used here of what a person does to his own self.
The Qur'an states the same outcome in almost the same words in a surah nearby, and there it is placed after the remembrance of the name of the Lord.

links.why: he has succeeded who purified himself, said with the same verb
the counterweight, that none of you would ever be pure without His favour

10.sense: The other half, and the verb is not destroyed but hidden. The failure named here is not a self that was killed off. It is one that was pushed down out of sight and left there to shrink.

notes.t: The root is d-s-s, to slip something in or push it under. The Qur'an uses the same verb for a man burying his infant daughter in the dust to be rid of the shame of her, which is the image behind this one word.
Khaba is the failure of a hope rather than of a plan. It is what you say about a man who set out expecting something and came back with nothing in his hands.

Both verbs in verses nine and ten are done by the person to himself. Nobody purifies him and nobody buries him, and the surah spends seven oaths establishing who made the self before it says what the self does with itself.

links.why: the same root used of a child hidden in the ground
he has failed who carries wrongdoing, the same verb for failure

11.sense: The rule about the two souls is now given a worked case. A people denied, and the verse names the cause of the denial as their own habit of going past the limit, which puts the conduct first and the creed second.

notes.t: Taghwa is from tagha, to overflow a bound. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the flood water rising past everything that had held it, which is the physical sense the moral one is built on.
The bi in bitaghwaha is causal: they denied by reason of their transgression. The verse is not saying they overstepped because they denied, which is the order most people assume.

Thamud were a real people with rock-cut dwellings on the trade road north of Medina, which is why the Qur'an can use them as a case rather than a parable. Their name appears in the surah before this one with no story attached at all.

links.why: the same people named beside Pharaoh with the story withheld
the fuller telling, from Salih's arrival to the she-camel

12.sense: One man stands up out of the group. He is not called the strongest or the bravest of them, though he was reckoned that at the time. He is called the most wretched, which is the outcome given before the act.

notes.t: Inbaʿatha is the seventh verbal form, which in Arabic carries being roused or being set going. He got to his feet, and the grammar leaves room for the crowd that put him there.
The Prophet ﷺ referred to this verse in a sermon and described the man who rose as one of standing among his people, protected by his clan, not a marginal figure.
notes.src: Bukhari records it in his tafsir of this surah, from ʿAbdullah ibn Zamʿa

notes.t: Ashqa is the superlative of shaqi, wretched, the standing opposite of saʿid, fortunate. The Qur'an sorts people into those two on the Day, so the word carries the final verdict into the middle of the story.

links.why: they called their companion and he took the blade and hamstrung her
they hamstrung her and defied the command of their Lord

words.g: and her turn at the water

13.sense: Salih is not named here. He is called the messenger of Allah, and his warning is four words long: the camel of Allah, and her drink. What was at stake was a rota at a well.

notes.t: Naqatallahi stands in the accusative, which in Arabic signals a dropped verb of warning. The sense is beware the camel of Allah, not this is the camel of Allah. The grammar makes it a shout rather than a description.
Suqya is a turn at the water, not water in general. The Qur'an spells the arrangement out elsewhere: one day for her and one day for them, each on a known day.
Leaving the messenger unnamed keeps the emphasis on the office rather than the man. A people were not refusing Salih, they were refusing someone sent, and that is the description the verse chooses.

links.why: the watering rota stated exactly, a drink for her and a drink for you
this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign, so leave her to eat

14.sense: Four actions joined by fa, the particle that means each one followed the last with nothing in between. Denial, then the killing, then the crushing, then the levelling. The verse moves at the speed the event moved.

notes.t: ʿAqara is to cut the hamstring so the animal goes down, and then to finish it. One man rose in verse twelve and here the verb is plural, so the whole people are made to carry what one pair of hands did.

Damdama is a doubled root, the shape Arabic reserves for repeated or heavy sound and motion. The lexicographers gloss it as bringing destruction down over a thing until nothing stands proud of the ground.
Sawwaha is the same verb used in verse seven of a soul being proportioned. The one act of levelling makes a self and unmakes a town, and the surah uses the word both ways within eight verses.

links.why: the shaking seized them and morning found them face down in their homes
the same verb used to make rather than to flatten

15.sense: The surah ends on what does not happen afterwards. A ruler who levels a town has to think about the next town, the reprisal and the account of it. The last line says that consideration has no place here.

notes.t: ʿUqba is what comes behind, from ʿaqib, a heel. The word is the trailing consequence of an act, the thing that follows it home.

Who the verb belongs to is read two ways: He does not fear the aftermath, meaning Allah, or he did not fear it, meaning the man who hamstrung her. Most of the exegetes take the first, which is why the surah closes on the doer rather than the deed.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir carry both, with the majority reading it of Allah

notes.t: Fifteen verses end on the same feminine ending, and this is the last of them. The surah is one long rhyme that opens on a sunrise and closes on an empty valley.

links.why: He is not questioned about what He does, and they are questioned
the doer of whatever He intends, the same point made from the other side

1.sense: The verb is passive, so something shakes the earth and the surah does not yet say what. Then the shaking is called hers, which separates it from every quake she has had before. This is the one that belongs to her.

notes.t: Zilzal is a doubled root, the shape Arabic uses for motion that repeats. The sound of the word is the thing it names, and the surah opens by making the reader say it.
Her shaking, with the possessive, is read as the quake appointed for her, the one she was always going to have. Every earthquake before it was a fragment of something; this is the whole of it.
The Qur'an names the quake of the Hour directly in another place and calls it an enormous thing, put at the very head of a surah as a warning.

links.why: the quake of the Hour named as the first thing in a surah
the earth convulsed at the same moment, told with a different verb

2.sense: Now the earth is the one acting. What she brings out is called her weights, the things she has been carrying all this time, and the word covers the dead in her ground and whatever else was put down into it.

notes.t: The verb is akhrajat, an active bringing out, not a losing or a spilling. The earth is described as handing something over rather than being emptied by force.
Thiql is a load. The Qur'an uses the same plural for the burdens that livestock carry to a distant town, which keeps the word in the register of freight rather than of horror.

Most exegetes read the burdens as the buried dead. Some include what else the ground holds, its metals and stores, and reports about the earth giving up its treasures near the end are discussed alongside this verse.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries the dead as the main reading and records the wider one

links.why: the earth casts out what is inside it and empties itself
when what is in the graves is turned out

3.sense: Two words of human speech are recorded, and they are a question. The entire response of the species to the end of the world is a puzzled phrase about the ground behaving oddly.

notes.t: Ma laha is low, ordinary spoken Arabic, the phrase used when a familiar thing starts acting strangely. The register is deliberate: no speech, no plea, just the noise a person makes when the floor moves.

Al-insan is definite and singular, the species standing there as one figure. The surah has three speakers in eight verses: man, the earth, and the Lord who instructed her, and this is the only one who does not know what is happening.
Some exegetes restrict the speaker to the denier, on the ground that a believer has been told what this is. Others leave it general, since shock is not a matter of creed.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the general reading and the restricted one

links.why: man will say that Day, where is the place to run
the eyes of those who denied fixed open at the sight of it

4.sense: The earth answers the question, and the answer is not an explanation of the quake. She reports what happened on her, which turns the ground under every act into the record of it.

notes.t: Haddatha is the plainest verb in Arabic for telling news, the root behind the word hadith. The ground is not giving evidence in a legal sense; it is talking, the way anyone talks about what they saw.

A report is transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ explained this verse as the earth testifying for or against each person about what was done on her surface. It comes through at-Tirmidhi and the chain is discussed by the critics.
notes.src: at-Tirmidhi reports it in his commentary on this surah and its chain is questioned

notes.t: The Qur'an already has skins, hands and feet speaking against their owners, so an earth that reports is inside a pattern rather than an exception to one.

links.why: they ask their own skins why they testified, and are answered
mouths sealed while hands speak and feet give evidence

5.sense: The reason the ground speaks is that it was told to. The verb is wahy, the same word used for what comes down to a prophet, and the earth is put on the receiving end of it.

notes.t: Awha in the Qur'an covers anything placed directly into a receiver: what is put to a bee about where to build, what is put to the mother of Musa about the basket, and what is put to a prophet. The word is about the channel, not the rank of the one receiving.

The usual Qur'anic construction is awha ila. Here it is awha laha, with a different preposition, and the exegetes note the change and read the lam as marking the earth's compliance rather than only the direction of the message.
notes.src: the commentators note the shift from ilā to the lām and explain it variously

notes.t: Rabbaka, your Lord, is the only second person address in the surah, and it is spoken to the Prophet ﷺ in the middle of a scene he is not in. The whole event is being narrated to one listener.

links.why: your Lord instructed the bee, the same verb for a creature under orders
He said to the sky and the earth, come willingly or unwillingly

6.sense: Sadara is the word for herds turning back from the water, the return leg after the crowding at the well. People come away in separate parties, and the reason given is not that they will be judged but that they will be shown.

notes.t: Sadara is the opposite of warada, going down to water. The Qur'an uses the pair at the well in Madyan, where Musa waits for the shepherds to draw off before he helps two women. The verse borrows a scene every desert listener had stood in.
Li-yuraw is passive: to be shown their deeds. They are not looking anything up. What they did is put in front of them by someone else, and the grammar gives them nothing to do but see.

Ashtat is scattered, separated into pieces that do not match. Everyone arrived at the same moment from the same ground and they leave it sorted, which is the first sign in the surah that the reckoning has already happened.

links.why: the same verb at a well, in its ordinary daily sense
they find everything they did present, and the record leaves nothing out

7.sense: The unit of measure is the smallest thing an Arab had a word for. And the verse does not say the deed is recorded or weighed or reported. It says the person sees it, which puts the act back in front of the eyes that once chose it.

notes.t: Dharra is explained by the lexicographers as the smallest ant, and also as the mote of dust you can only see in a shaft of light through a doorway. Either way it is chosen because it is the limit of what a person can notice.

The Prophet ﷺ was asked about donkeys and answered that nothing had come down to him about them except this one comprehensive verse, and then recited it. The report is well known and appears in more than one collection.
notes.src: Bukhari records it in the Book of Watering and again in his tafsir; also in Malik's Muwatta

notes.t: Mithqal is a weight, the same word used where the Qur'an describes the scales set up for the Day and says that even a mustard seed will be brought.

links.why: the just scales, down to the weight of a mustard seed
Allah does not wrong by so much as the weight of a speck

8.sense: The mirror of the verse before, changed by one word. The surah that opened with the whole planet coming apart closes on a quantity too small to be noticed, and both halves end with the same verb: he sees it.

notes.t: The two verses are identical except for khayran and sharran. Good is put first, and the Qur'an does that consistently when it pairs the two, so the reader meets the promise before the warning.
The surah moves from the largest event it can describe to the smallest act it can name, and joins them in eight verses. The quake exists so that the speck can be produced.
A report circulates that this surah equals half the Qur'an. It comes through at-Tirmidhi with a weak chain and the critics did not accept it, so it should not be repeated as the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ words.
notes.src: at-Tirmidhi in the chapter on the merits of the Qur'an; the chain is weak and was not acted upon

links.why: the Day each self finds what it did of good present, and what it did of evil
a soul will know what it has put forward, at the end of a similar list
